strengths: The paper addresses an important and relatively underexplored problem: extracting rule-centric business logic with conditional and parallel dependencies rather than only temporal action sequences. This is relevant to NLP, procedural text understanding, and business process automation.

The proposed annotation schema is intuitive and potentially useful: rules are represented as Condition–Action pairs, with conditions decomposed into slot type, logical judgment, and reference value, and with sequential, conditional, and parallel dependencies.

BPRF contributes a Chinese cross-domain resource of 50 documents and 326 rules spanning domains such as banking, healthcare, e-commerce, and manufacturing. The combination of domain-expert annotation, separate verification, and reported agreement scores is a positive feature.

The reported agreement is high: ICC 0.904 for text-quality assessment and Fleiss’ kappa 0.911 for the BIO-based annotation, suggesting substantial consistency in the parts of the annotation that were directly evaluated.

ExIde is a clearly structured two-stage framework that separates business-rule extraction from dependency identification. The five prompt variants provide a useful exploration of implicit mapping, explicit mapping, clarified input, logical judgment, and pseudo-code support.

The empirical comparison covers 12 closed- and open-source LLMs and supplies component-level results for span extraction, logical-judgment classification, and dependency classification. The appendix includes concrete examples and prompt templates, which aids understanding and future reuse.
The case studies help interpret model behavior, especially the comparison between DeepSeek v3 and reasoning-oriented models such as DeepSeek r1 on subtle dependency distinctions.
weaknesses: The central evaluation does not directly measure end-to-end rule-flow extraction. NER-style F1 for Slot Type, Reference Value, and Action spans does not evaluate whether the model assembles the correct complete Condition–Action tuples, links attributes correctly, counts rules correctly, or produces the correct dependency graph. Tuple-level, rule-level, and graph-level metrics are needed to support the paper’s main effectiveness claim.

The dependency evaluation is ambiguous. It is unclear whether all possible rule pairs are classified, how the dominant no-relation class is handled, and whether Macro-F1 is computed over only the three positive dependency types. With only 24 conditional and 33 parallel examples, excluding or under-reporting no-relation pairs could substantially inflate performance. The paper should report candidate-pair counts, per-class precision/recall/F1, confusion matrices, and both edge-detection and edge-classification results.

It is also unclear whether Stage 2 uses gold rules or rules predicted in Stage 1. If predicted rules are used, error propagation should be analyzed; if gold rules are used, the dependency result is an oracle experiment rather than an end-to-end evaluation. Both settings should be reported.

The dataset is small for a broad benchmark claim, and its composition is under-specified. The paper does not report the proportion of real versus ChatGPT-generated documents, per-domain document/rule distributions, train/test or fixed-test splits, duplication controls, or contamination checks. Synthetic documents generated from the annotation schema may be easier and more templatic than naturally occurring business texts.

Agreement evidence is incomplete for the most difficult annotations. The reported kappa appears to concern BIO span annotation, while no dedicated agreement statistics are provided for logical-judgment labels or dependency edges. Adjudication guidelines and disagreement resolution procedures should also be described more fully.

The logical-judgment labels are highly imbalanced: 205 contains and 86 equal-to labels, but only 1, 17, 16, and 1 examples for the remaining four judgment types. Aggregate Macro-F1 therefore hides potentially unstable performance on the numeric comparisons that motivate the schema. Per-class results are essential.

Experimental robustness and reproducibility are limited. The paper does not report multiple runs, random seeds, temperature or decoding settings, confidence intervals, statistical significance, parsing failures, exact model versions, or API access dates. This is especially important for prompt-sensitive closed-source models and a 50-document test set.

Some empirical claims are stronger than the results support. For example, Prompt 1 is said to consistently achieve the highest NER performance, but several models perform better with Prompt 3 or Prompt 4 in Table 4. The dependency and logical-judgment scores are also moderate for many models, so claims about reliable business-rule analysis should be tempered.

The technical novelty is relatively incremental. ExIde primarily combines two-stage prompting with prompt-engineering variants, and the paper does not compare against strong non-LLM baselines, fine-tuned extractors, self-consistency decoding, or existing business-process/BPMN extraction systems adapted to the dataset.

The annotation schema captures only local, pairwise dependencies and relatively simple Condition–Action rules. It does not naturally represent compound or nested conditions, global constraints, exclusions, cardinalities, or richer process structures. The authors acknowledge some of this, but it limits the benchmark’s fidelity to real business processes.

Although the authors intend to release the dataset after acceptance, the current submission does not provide the dataset, annotation guidelines, or code for inspection. Together with the missing inference details, this makes the reported results difficult to reproduce at present.
There are minor presentation issues, including typos such as “staisfied” and “econstruct,” and the dense tables would benefit from per-domain and per-label breakdowns.

strengths: The paper targets a relevant problem at the intersection of NLP and business process management: extracting condition-driven business rules, rather than only temporally ordered action sequences.
The annotation schema is fairly explicit, representing rules as <Condition, Action> pairs and distinguishing sequential, conditional, and parallel dependencies.
The BPRF dataset covers several domains and includes Chinese business texts, which is a potentially useful contribution for multilingual business-process NLP.
The authors use multiple expert annotators and verifiers, report agreement statistics, and include many concrete annotation examples and prompt templates.
The evaluation is broad in model coverage, comparing 12 closed- and open-source LLMs across five prompt variants and three subproblems.
The limitations section candidly acknowledges dataset size, synthetic-data bias, prompt sensitivity, and the restriction to pairwise dependencies.
weaknesses: The dataset is small for a benchmark—only 50 documents and 326 rules—and the paper does not report how many documents or rules are real versus ChatGPT-generated. Domain-level counts and provenance are also missing, making distribution bias and generalizability hard to judge.

The reported agreement is not fully persuasive. The ICC of 0.904 mainly concerns text-quality ratings, while the token-level Fleiss kappa of 0.911 can be inflated by the large number of outside/O tokens. Span-level or entity-level agreement, adjudication procedures, and annotation-guideline details are needed.

The main extraction claim is evaluated as token-level NER, but correct business-rule extraction also requires assembling Slot Type, Logical Judgement, Reference Value, and Action into valid tuples. High span F1 does not demonstrate correct tuple or rule construction.

The evaluation omits important details: whether NER matching is exact or partial, precision and recall, parsing failures, variance across documents, confidence intervals, and statistical significance of differences among prompts.

Logical Judgement classes are sparse and highly imbalanced—for example, very few instances express less-than, greater-than, or related comparisons—so Macro-F1 is unstable. No per-class results or confusion analysis are provided.

For dependency classification, all rule pairs produce a dominant 'no relationship' class, but no classwise performance or majority-class baseline is reported. It is also unclear whether Table 6 uses gold rules or Stage-1 predicted rules, so error propagation is not controlled.

The definition of sequential dependency is inconsistent. Section 3 defines it as one rule occurring before another, while the Stage-2 prompt requires a direct relation with no intermediate rule. Non-adjacent but temporally ordered pairs are therefore labeled 'no relation,' changing the task semantics.

There are no strong baselines beyond prompted LLMs, such as prior business-process extraction methods, fine-tuned sequence models, or graph-based systems. The paper also does not define fixed train/dev/test splits or a reproducible leaderboard setup.

Reproducibility is limited by data being promised only after acceptance, no stated code release, unspecified decoding parameters and API access dates, and reliance on nondeterministic web-based models.

The conclusions overstate the results: NER performance is strong, but Logical Judgement and dependency scores remain modest, and no downstream decision-support or process-execution utility is demonstrated.

The technical novelty is relatively limited because ExIde is primarily a two-stage prompting pipeline and closely related prior work already extracts Chinese process conditions, roles, dependencies, and BPMN-style structures.
The paper needs polishing: it contains typos such as 'eoustuct' and 'staisfied,' duplicated or inconsistent references, and several table details that require clearer explanation.

strengths: The paper addresses an underexplored and practically important gap: moving from action-sequence extraction to rule-centric business-process modeling with explicit conditions, actions, and inter-rule dependencies.

The BPRF dataset contributes a densely annotated Chinese benchmark with a clear schema for Condition attributes, Action, and sequential, conditional, and parallel dependencies across several business domains.

Dataset construction includes multiple annotators, expert verification, and quality assessment; the reported ICC of 0.904 and Fleiss' kappa of 0.911 indicate strong agreement for the evaluated annotation layers.

ExIde is intuitive and decomposes the problem into business-rule extraction and dependency identification. The five prompt variants provide a useful controlled comparison of implicit mapping, explicit alignment, clarified input, logical reasoning, and pseudo-code.
The evaluation covers a broad set of 12 closed- and open-source LLMs and reports both extraction and classification performance, supplemented by qualitative case studies.

The findings are practically informative: simpler implicit alignment appears strongest for span extraction, explicit logical guidance helps logical-judgment classification, and reasoning-oriented models tend to perform better on dependency identification.
The appendix provides detailed prompts and examples, and the authors plan to release the annotated dataset after acceptance.
weaknesses: The benchmark is small: only 50 documents and 326 rules. The domain distribution and the proportion of real versus ChatGPT-generated documents are not clearly reported, which limits assessment of coverage and ecological validity.

Reproducibility is only partially supported. The paper does not specify model versions or access dates, decoding parameters, temperatures, number of runs, random seeds, output parsing, exact matching rules, or fixed evaluation splits; closed models were accessed through web versions.

The reported agreement does not cover all modeled structures. The ICC concerns text quality and the kappa concerns NER-style annotations, but agreement on condition-action tuple pairing, logical judgments, and dependency labels is not separately established.

The rule-extraction evaluation is not fully end-to-end. High NER F1 on Slot Type, Reference Value, and Action does not guarantee that these components are correctly grouped into Condition-Action rules or connected to the correct logical judgment.

The classification protocol needs more detail. It is unclear whether dependency classification uses gold rules or rules predicted in stage one, how all rule pairs are constructed, and how the large expected 'no relation' class is distributed and scored.

Several label classes are extremely rare, especially logical judgments such as 'less than' with one instance. Aggregate Macro-F1 can therefore be unstable, and per-class precision, recall, and F1 are needed, particularly for conditional and parallel dependencies.
The paper reports F1 scores without precision and recall, confidence intervals, or significance tests, so small differences between models and prompts should not be interpreted too strongly.

The methodological novelty is relatively limited: ExIde is primarily a prompt-engineering pipeline, and pairwise dependency classification does not yet model global graph consistency or complex process constraints.
The broad claims about real-world automation and interpretability should be tempered because of the synthetic-data component, limited scale, and the absence of non-LLM or fine-tuned baselines.

strengths: Addresses a relevant and underexplored NLP problem: extracting rule-centric business processes with conditional branching, parallel execution, and inter-rule dependencies, rather than only linear action flows.

BREX is a reasonably large and broad benchmark, containing 409 documents, 2,855 expert-annotated rules, and coverage of more than 30 vertical domains, with a clear condition–action representation and typed dependency graph.

The annotation schema is well documented, with formal definitions, illustrative examples, multi-stage expert verification, and detailed appendices that help clarify the intended task and rule granularity.

ExIde provides a practical zero-fine-tuning framework and a useful decomposition between atomic rule extraction and global dependency reasoning. The comparison of five prompting strategies across 13 LLMs gives a broad empirical picture.
The paper includes complexity and robustness analyses, qualitative failure cases, an explicit limitations section, and a thorough ethical statement, which strengthen transparency and interpretation.
weaknesses: Several dataset-construction details are missing or underspecified: the number and proportion of synthetic documents/rules, domain-level distribution, source lists, expert qualifications, adjudication procedure, licensing, data splits, and the promised code/dataset URL. These omissions limit reproducibility and auditability.

The reliability of the central dependency annotations is not directly established. The reported Fleiss' kappa of 0.901 is computed after projecting annotations into BIO/NER spans and therefore does not directly measure agreement on edge existence or on Sequential/Conditional/Parallel labels. The ICC of 0.892 concerns text-quality ratings rather than graph annotation reliability.

Evaluation is component-oriented rather than task-oriented. Separate NER F1 scores for slots, values, and actions and operator F1 do not show exact condition–action tuple accuracy, while pairwise dependency F1 does not measure complete graph accuracy, topology, or graph-edit performance. Precision, recall, macro/micro averaging, and the prevalence of the None class are also not clearly reported.

It is unclear whether Stage II is evaluated using gold rules or model-extracted rules. If predicted rules are used, the paper should isolate extraction error from dependency-reasoning error and report cascaded end-to-end performance; if gold rules are used, the end-to-end ExIde result is not demonstrated.

The graph is assembled from independent pairwise classifications without global consistency checks, transitivity constraints, or conflict resolution. This is not sufficient to establish that the reconstructed output is a globally coherent rule-flow graph.

Prompt 5 is described as 'executable grounding,' but the generated pseudo-code is not actually executed, compiled, tested, or given execution feedback. The evidence supports a code-like representational bias more strongly than true executable grounding.

The claimed advantage of P5 is modest on average and is not supported by significance tests or confidence intervals. There are also model- and density-specific reversals, including degraded precision in high-density documents, so the abstract-level claim that executable grounding consistently or significantly outperforms other strategies is stronger than the evidence warrants.

The reasoning-model comparison is suggestive but not fully controlled across all model families, and the gains are sometimes small. Additional simple discourse-heuristic, supervised, or fine-tuned baselines would help contextualize the reported LLM results.

Synthetic documents generated with Gemini 2.5 Pro may introduce model-family stylistic biases; without a detailed proportion and style analysis, the 'real-world' characterization of the augmented benchmark should be more carefully qualified.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and practically relevant NLP problem: extracting condition–action business rules and their non-linear dependencies from regulatory documents, rather than only linear action flows.

BREX is a substantial and potentially useful resource, with 409 documents, 2,855 expert-annotated rules, a formal condition schema, and explicit Sequential, Conditional, and Parallel dependency relations across many domains.

The empirical study is broad, evaluating 13 LLMs from five model families under five prompting strategies, with separate extraction and dependency-reasoning stages, complexity analyses, and detailed qualitative error cases.
The manuscript is generally well organized and readable, and the appendix supplies useful definitions, annotation examples, dataset statistics, prompts, and ethical discussion.

The finding that code-like intermediate representations and reasoning-oriented models may be especially helpful for branching and concurrent dependencies is interesting and relevant to logic-intensive information extraction.
weaknesses: Benchmark provenance and reproducibility are under-specified. The artifact URL is blank in the submitted manuscript, and the paper does not provide the real-versus-synthetic document/rule counts, source or domain distribution, evaluation split, few-shot example separation, model versions, decoding parameters, or random seeds.

The reported agreement evidence is indirect. ICC 0.892 concerns text-quality ratings, while Fleiss' Kappa 0.901 is computed on a projection to token-level NER annotations for an unspecified subset. Neither directly measures agreement on atomic rule tuples or typed dependency graphs; annotator backgrounds, adjudication procedures, and confidence intervals are also missing.

The evaluation does not fully assess the stated end-to-end task. NER-style F1 for slots/actions and operator classification do not measure whether components are correctly grouped into condition–action rules. Pairwise dependency F1 likewise does not establish that the reconstructed graph is globally coherent or correct; the paper should report tuple-level F1, edge precision/recall, graph-level metrics, and clarify macro/micro averaging and treatment of the None class.

Claims that executable grounding 'significantly outperforms' standard prompts are overstated. Its average advantage is very small and is not consistent across all models, while no statistical significance tests, variance estimates, or repeated-run analyses are provided.

The reasoning-model comparison is not fully controlled. Different model sizes, versions, and possibly different Stage-I extraction quality may confound the apparent dependency-reasoning gains. Stage II should be evaluated both with gold rules and with model-extracted rules to isolate graph-reasoning ability.

The term 'executable grounding' is not substantiated: the intermediate representation is pseudo-code, but the paper provides no executor, compilation checks, execution traces, or semantic equivalence evaluation to verify that it is executable.

Graph construction treats rule pairs independently and then assembles an adjacency matrix, without reporting constraints or error analysis for cycles, symmetric Parallel edges, inconsistent directionality, transitivity, or conflicting predictions. Local pairwise accuracy may therefore yield an invalid global flow graph.

The use of Gemini-generated synthetic texts is a potential source of bias, especially because Gemini models are also evaluated. Results should be stratified by real versus synthetic documents, and the proportion and construction of synthetic data should be fully disclosed.

The methodological contribution is primarily a prompt-engineering pipeline, with limited comparison to non-LLM rule-extraction systems, entailment-based relation baselines, or constrained graph-decoding approaches. The narrow operator/relation schema also limits coverage of exceptions, temporal constraints, uncertainty, and richer logical formalisms.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and practically relevant NLP problem: moving beyond linear action extraction toward rule-centric business flows containing conditional branching and parallel dependencies.

BREX is a substantial and broadly scoped resource, with 409 documents, 2,855 expert-annotated rules, and coverage of more than 30 vertical domains. The reported prevalence of conditional and parallel relations supports the need for the benchmark.

The annotation schema is explicit and useful, representing atomic rules as condition–action pairs and labeling Sequential, Conditional, and Parallel dependencies. The multi-stage expert annotation and verification process is also appropriate for a gold-standard benchmark.

ExIde provides a practical no-finetuning solution and systematically compares five prompting strategies spanning implicit alignment, traceability, input clarification, logic definitions, and pseudo-code grounding.

The empirical study is broad, evaluating 13 LLMs from several model families and sizes, and includes both extraction performance and dependency-reasoning performance. The complexity and robustness analyses add useful insight beyond aggregate scores.
The paper is generally clear, well organized, and supported by illustrative figures, detailed prompt appendices, an ethical statement, and a candid discussion of limitations.
weaknesses: The claim that executable grounding 'significantly' outperforms other strategies is not fully supported. The aggregate gains are small—for example, average NER F1 rises from 0.879 for P1 to 0.881 for P5—and P5 is not best for every model. Statistical significance tests, confidence intervals, or paired comparisons are missing.

The reported Kappa of 0.901 is based on a projected NER representation and mainly evaluates spans and components, not the existence or labels of rule-to-rule dependency edges. Edge-level and graph-structured inter-annotator agreement are still needed to validate the dependency annotations.

It is unclear whether Stage II uses gold-standard rules or rules predicted in Stage I. No explicit end-to-end results are reported for constructing a dependency graph from extracted rules, so the full ExIde pipeline is not directly evaluated.

Pairwise dependency predictions are independently classified and then assembled into an adjacency matrix. The paper does not describe global consistency constraints, cycle handling, transitivity checks, or graph-level metrics such as exact graph match or edge precision/recall.

Several dataset-construction and reproducibility details are absent: the exact number or proportion of synthetic documents and rules, per-domain distribution, source and license information, data splits, annotator backgrounds, adjudication procedure, API versions, and decoding settings. The abstract also does not show a concrete resource URL.

The term 'executable grounding' is somewhat overstated because the pseudo-code representations are not actually executed, syntax-checked, or evaluated in a downstream rule engine. Their executability and operational utility remain unverified.

Component-level NER F1 and logical-operator F1 may overestimate task success because they do not necessarily verify correct condition–action pairing, rule cardinality, tuple consistency, or the complete rule set. A tuple-level or end-task metric would strengthen the evaluation.

The baseline comparison is limited to variants of the authors’ prompting framework. Comparisons with supervised information-extraction methods, process-mining approaches, or BPMN/DMN-oriented systems would better establish ExIde’s practical advantage.

The effect of synthetic augmentation is not isolated. Because synthetic texts were generated with Gemini 2.5 Pro and may share stylistic patterns with evaluated LLMs, results should be reported separately for real-world and augmented documents.
